title: Pull, Don't Push: Hand Over the Why With the Work
summary: Deadlines get work done. A real reason gets people to care about it. What motivation research says about push and pull, and how to hand off work with its why.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Two ways to hand off the same task. In the first, a ticket lands in a teammate's queue: clear title, acceptance criteria, a due date. In the second, you spend two minutes at their desk explaining what the work is for, who's stuck until it ships, and why you thought of them. Same task, same deadline. Only one of them is still on their mind on the bus home.

Tickets aren't the problem here. Every team needs them. This post is about the two extra minutes: why they move people further than the ticket does, what the research says about it, and how to keep them honest.

Push sets the floor, pull does the rest

Call them push and pull. Push runs on position: deadlines, requirements, KPIs, the review at the end of the quarter. Pull runs on reasons: people move toward the work because they can see why it matters and they trust the person asking. Real work needs both. A clear deadline is a favor to everyone on the team.

Push has a ceiling, though, and motivation research is fairly clear about where it sits. In self-determination theory, Richard Ryan and Edward Deci compare people who are "merely externally controlled" with people who actually endorse what they're doing. The second group shows more interest, excitement and confidence, and it shows up as better performance, persistence and creativity, even when both groups feel equally capable (Ryan and Deci, 2000). Push mostly buys you the first kind. You get exactly what the deadline asks for. Whatever else the team had in them, you never find out.

Think of a teenager told to tidy their room or lose the phone. You'll get a room that passes inspection and a closed door. The day they tidy it without being asked is the day it became their room, and nobody can put a due date on that day.

Two hands on the reins

American Sign Language has a neat picture of push. The sign for MANAGE (also used for "control") looks like two hands holding a horse's reins and pulling back on them in turns (Lifeprint ASL dictionary). Keeping a strong animal on the road is a real skill, and some weeks it's exactly the job.

A version that goes around leadership circles adds a lovelier second half: that the sign for LEAD is two arms rocking a baby. I couldn't trace that half to any source, so treat it as a parable. The point holds up anyway. Hands on the reins keep the horse on the road. They don't make it want to go anywhere.

Why pull takes longer

Push is fast and easy to see. A deadline exists the moment you set it, and everyone can measure against it. Pull builds up slowly, through how you frame the work, the reasons you give and the trust you earn over months of ordinary 1:1s and PR threads.

The research hints at what builds it. In a lab experiment by Deci, Eghrari, Patrick and Leone, people did a dull task. Those who got a meaningful rationale, along with support for their autonomy and for feeling connected, took the task on as their own more fully. Controlling setups produced less of that, and what little they produced tended to be the pressured kind, done out of guilt or to look good (summarized in Ryan and Deci, 2000). In sprint terms: say why, let people choose how, and treat them as teammates. None of that ever shows up on a burndown chart.

So for a while, pull looks like nothing is happening. No ticket closes because you explained the reason behind it. Then one sprint the team starts flagging problems before you ask, and you realize the work was happening all along.

Let the team meet the person the work is for

You've probably seen this one on a slide: "If you want to build a ship, don't drum up people to collect wood... teach them to long for the endless immensity of the sea." It usually comes credited to Antoine de Saint-Exupéry. Quote Investigator found no close match in his writing, only a passage on a similar theme in Citadelle, and suspects someone paraphrased it later and pinned it on him (Quote Investigator). Great line, shaky source. Luckily the idea inside it has much better evidence.

Adam Grant and his colleagues studied paid callers at a public university's fundraising call center, a job with a lot of hang-ups. One group spent about five minutes with a scholarship student whose funding came from those calls. Over the next month, those callers spent more than twice as many minutes on the phone, and their weekly average raised went from $185.94 to $503.22 (Knowledge at Wharton; paper: Grant et al., 2007). Nobody gave them a new KPI. They had met the person on the other end of the work.

For an engineering team this is cheap to set up. Sit in on a support call. Read the raw customer ticket instead of the summary. Bring the shop owner's screenshot to sprint planning. Then the "why" in your handoff is something the team has already seen with their own eyes, and you don't have to sell it.

When pull goes bad

Pull turns into manipulation the moment the reason is fake. Hang the work on a "why" you don't believe and people figure it out sooner or later, and the trust you thought you were saving drains away. If the truth is "it's a compliance deadline, it's boring, sorry", say that. People take a boring true reason much better than an inspiring made-up one.

When to push, when to pull

Push for the floor: who owns what, dates you've committed to, anything touching security or safety, the few rules that really aren't up for debate. Pull for everything above it: the extra care, the edge case someone catches on their own, the idea nobody asked for. A team on push alone does what it's told and slowly runs out of steam. A team on pull alone is fired up and a bit all over the place. A big part of leading is noticing which one this particular week needs.

Try this week

  • Add three sentences to the next task you hand off: what it's for, who's waiting on it, and why this person.
  • If the honest reason is "we're required to," say exactly that.
  • Get one teammate closer to a real user: a support call, a raw ticket, a screenshot from the field.
  • Scroll back through your last five requests and count how many came with a reason.

This is the last post in the leadership series, and one idea kept coming back across all five: the people side of leading turned out to be most of the actual work. If you're starting here, the series opens with Over-Managed and Under-Led, and the post on signals and messages pairs well with this one.

faqs.q: What's the difference between push and pull leadership?
faqs.a: Push runs on position: deadlines, requirements, KPIs, reviews. Pull runs on reasons and trust, so people move toward the work because they see why it matters. Real work needs both. Push alone tends to get you exactly what was asked for, while self-determination research links motivation people actually endorse with better performance, persistence and creativity.

faqs.q: Does explaining the why really change how people work?
faqs.a: There's good evidence it can. In a study by Adam Grant and colleagues, paid fundraising callers at a public university spent about five minutes with a scholarship student their calls helped fund. Over the next month they spent more than twice as many minutes on the phone, and their weekly average raised went from $185.94 to $503.22.

faqs.q: Is the sign-language story about reins and a cradle true?
faqs.a: Half of it checks out. In American Sign Language, MANAGE is signed like two hands holding a horse's reins. The claim that LEAD is signed by rocking a baby circulates in leadership talks, but I couldn't find a source for it, so treat that part as a parable.

faqs.q: Isn't connecting work to meaning just manipulation?
faqs.a: It becomes manipulation when the reason is fake. If you attach a why you don't believe, people notice sooner or later and trust drops. When the honest reason is dull, like a compliance deadline, say so. A boring true reason lands better than an inspiring invented one.

faqs.q: When should a leader push and when should they pull?
faqs.a: Push for the floor: clear ownership, committed dates, security and safety, and the few rules that aren't up for debate. Pull for everything above that floor: extra care, edge cases people catch on their own, ideas nobody asked for. A team on push alone gets tired, and a team on pull alone gets a bit chaotic.
